ctf_name: Module 07 - Docker and Host Escape in 5G Simulations
description: This beginner-friendly guide provides a step-by-step walkthrough on exploiting and defending against Docker container escapes in a simulated 5G environment using Open5GS and UERANSIM. Docker containers virtualize applications but share the host kernel, making them lighter than VMs but potentially vulnerable if misconfigured (e.g., privileged mode). You'll learn red team techniques to escape a container and access the host filesystem, then blue team defenses using Linux capabilities to restrict privileges without full root access. Educational focus: Understand container isolation, privileged risks, mount commands, chroot, and secure configs. Assumes the 5G lab stack is running with Docker Compose files (ngc.yml, gnb1.yml, gnb2.yml). Flags prove key observations and mitigations.

steps.action: Red Team: Examine Docker Compose Files for Privileged Mode
steps.command: cat ngc.yml gnb1.yml gnb2.yml | grep -i mode (or manually review files for 'mode' settings in amf/upf services)
steps.expected_output: Lines show 'mode: true' or similar under services like amf and upf, indicating privileged mode.
steps.explanation: Docker Compose simplifies running multiple containers (e.g., AMF for mobility, UPF for data routing) with one command like 'docker compose -f ngc.yml up -d' (-f specifies file, -d runs in background, up starts). Privileged mode gives containers full host access, like root superpowers—great for testing but dangerous in production as it bypasses isolation. Analogy: Giving a guest full house keys instead of just a room key. This step identifies the vulnerability. Flag: privileged_mode
next_steps: Enter AMF Container and Check for Docker Environment

steps.action: Red Team: Verify Docker Environment in AMF Container
steps.command: docker exec -it open5gs-and-ueransim-amf-1 bash; then cat /proc/self/mountinfo | grep docker
steps.expected_output: Output shows mounts for /etc/resolv.conf, /etc/hostname, /etc/hosts, and a line with /dev/mapper/ubuntu--vg-ubuntu--lv (host filesystem) plus a container ID hash after /var/lib/docker/containers/.
steps.explanation: /proc/self/mountinfo lists mounted filesystems. Seeing 'docker' confirms containerization. These three files (/etc/resolv.conf for DNS, /etc/hostname for name, /etc/hosts for IP mappings) are often bind-mounted from host for networking. /dev/mapper/ubuntu--vg-ubuntu--lv is the host's main disk (LVM logical volume) exposed due to privileged mode. Analogy: Peeking at the building blueprint to confirm you're in an apartment, not the whole house. The container ID is unique per container. Flag: /dev/mapper/ubuntu--vg-ubuntu--lv
next_steps: Mount Host Dev to Container Dev

steps.action: Red Team: Mount Host Dev Directory Inside Container
steps.expected_output: No output if successful; now /dev in container mirrors host's device files.
steps.explanation: 'mount -t devtmpfs' attaches a temporary filesystem of type devtmpfs (device files) to /dev. /dev holds special files for hardware (e.g., disks, random generators). In privileged mode, this exposes host devices to the container, allowing further escapes. Analogy: Copying the house's tool shed into your room so you can pick locks. Education: Dev nodes enable access to peripherals; pseudo-devices like /dev/random provide randomness for security.

steps.action: Red Team: Mount Host Filesystem and Access Flag
steps.command: mount /dev/mapper/ubuntu--vg-ubuntu--lv /mnt; then chroot /mnt /bin/bash (optional for full host shell); cat /flag.txt
steps.expected_output: Host files accessible at /mnt; cat shows flag.txt contents (generated dynamically).
steps.explanation: 'mount /dev/mapper/... /mnt' attaches the host's root disk to /mnt in container, giving full host file access. chroot /mnt /bin/bash changes root to /mnt and starts bash, making container act as host. Analogy: Drilling a hole to the main house from your room and stepping through. Education: Once escaped, attackers can read secrets, install malware, or pivot. Flag is in /flag.txt on host root, proving escape. Flag: contents of flag.txt file (will be generated by the container when mounted)

steps.action: Blue Team: Stop Stack and Edit ngc.yml to Remove Privileged Mode
steps.command: docker compose down (stop stack); then nano ngc.yml (comment out 'privileged: true' with # in amf/upf sections)
steps.expected_output: Stack stops; edited file no longer has active privileged mode.
steps.explanation: docker compose down safely stops all containers. Privileged mode is insecure as it grants all capabilities (privileges). Removing it hardens security but may break functions needing specific access (e.g., network config). Analogy: Taking away the master key and giving only needed room keys. Education: Use least privilege principle—grant only what's essential.

steps.action: Blue Team: Add Specific Linux Capabilities to ngc.yml
steps.command: In ngc.yml under amf/upf: add 'cap_add: - NET_ADMIN' (from man capabilities or https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/capabilities.7.html)
steps.expected_output: Updated amf section: image: ..., command: ..., #privileged: true, cap_add: - NET_ADMIN, restart: ...
steps.explanation: Capabilities divide root powers into granular ones (e.g., CAP_NET_ADMIN for network interfaces). NET_ADMIN allows admin ops like interface config without full root. Check 'man capabilities' for list. Analogy: Instead of full access, give just the key to the network room. Education: This maintains functionality (e.g., for 5G networking) while blocking escapes. Flag: CAP_NET_ADMIN

steps.action: Blue Team: Restart Stack and Attempt Attack Again
steps.command: docker compose -f ngc.yml up -d; then repeat red team steps in AMF: mount -t devtmpfs devtmpfs /dev
steps.expected_output: Mount fails with permission denied error.
steps.explanation: up -d restarts securely. Without privileged, container lacks CAP_SYS_ADMIN (for mounts) so escape fails. Analogy: Trying to pick the lock but the tools are confiscated. Education: Always audit configs; tools like Docker Bench Security check for issues. Flag: mount: /dev: permission denied.
